label: sec:exp-mod-reduce
title: Reduction of mod Operations
html:
The translation TRANS produces a mod by exp(2,k) for every arithmetic bit-vector operation at width k. Removing redundant mod operations is very useful, as every removed mod removes a non-linear operation from the formula. For operations at the same width, the translated formula therefore contains nested mod operations by the same power of two, of which only the outermost one is needed. [7] removes them by the rules +rri​, −rri​ and ⋅rri​ of Table 4, which are stated for pow2​. We generalize them to a modulus exp(s,k) for an arbitrary positive base s, under the guard s>0, which keeps the modulus positive. In multi-width formulas, the widths of nested operations differ, e.g., extract of a sum translates to ((x+y)mod2m)mod2k with k≤m, so the exponents of the inner and the outer modulus differ and the rules of [7], which require syntactically identical widths, do not apply. For this case, we use the rules of [35], which are stated for powers of two with different exponents, and generalize them to an arbitrary positive base s. All rules require s>0, so that exp(s,k) is a positive divisor of exp(s,m) for 0≤k≤m. A negative base is excluded since, e.g., rule div-div does not hold for negative divisors: for s=−4, i=j=1 and x=−17, the left-hand side is (−17div−4)div−4=5div−4=−1, while the right-hand side is −17div16=−2. In [35], these rules are equalities that are applied in both directions. We orient each of them in the direction that decreases the number of mod and div operations, so that every rewrite step removes at least one of them. These rules are applied by a learned-rewrite pass on the translated formula, which applies a rule only where the constraints of the formula entail its side condition on the order of the exponents.

Example. The multi-width Hydra benchmark opt_2751 checks the optimization trunc(zext(v4​)−zext(v1​))⇒v4​−v1​, where v1​ and v4​ have width r, the extensions have width s, and r<s. It asserts extractr−1,0​(zexts−r​(v4​)−zexts−r​(v1​))=v4​−v1​. Since a zero extension does not change the integer value, the translation yields ((v4​−v1​)modexp(2,s))modexp(2,r)=(v4​−v1​)modexp(2,r). The two sides have different moduli, so the rules of [7] do not apply. The width constraints entail 1≤r and r<s, i.e., 0≤r≤s, so mod-mod-outer rewrites the left-hand side to (v4​−v1​)modexp(2,r), and the disequality becomes false during preprocessing. Without this rule, each of the three mod operations is purified into a fresh variable with a non-linear defining constraint, and cvc5 does not solve the benchmark within the time limit.
